Diffusion Models (Image and Video Generation)

A diffusion model generates data such as images, video or molecular structures by learning to undo noise. Training teaches a network to remove a small amount of Gaussian noise from corrupted samples, and generation starts from pure noise and applies that denoiser many times until a clean sample appears.

1Overview

Why it matters

Diffusion models are the recipe behind Stable Diffusion and SDXL-style image generators, and the same recipe has been applied to video, global weather forecasts and protein design. If you build, host or pay for a generative image or video feature, the settings you meet every day are properties of this recipe: the number of sampling steps, the guidance scale, the scheduler and the size of the latent image.

Without the mechanism in your head, these settings look like superstitions. With it, you can estimate how many network calls one image costs, see why a distilled model can run in one step, predict why a very high guidance scale produces burnt-looking pictures, and read a model card or paper without guessing what "predicts the noise" or "works in latent space" means. ML engineers, product engineers who estimate latency and cost, and anyone evaluating generated media benefit from knowing it.

Before you start

  • Autoencoders and Generative Models (VAE, GAN)Advanced
  • Attention and TransformersAdvanced

What you will be able to do

  • Compute a noised sample at any timestep from a clean sample, a noise draw and the schedule value alpha-bar, and check it by hand.
  • Explain why the network is trained to predict the added noise, and compute the simplified training loss for one example.
  • Carry out one reverse sampling step by hand and say what each term in the update does.
  • Describe how latent diffusion, cross-attention text conditioning and classifier-free guidance combine in a text-to-image pipeline.
  • Compare U-Net and transformer denoisers, including what each receives as input.
  • Predict how the number of sampling steps, the guidance scale and the sampler change cost, latency and output quality.

Key terms

Forward process
The fixed, unlearned procedure that turns a clean sample into noise by adding a little Gaussian noise at each of T steps.
Reverse process
The learned procedure that starts from noise and removes it step by step; running it is called sampling.
Noise schedule
The list of noise amounts beta_1 to beta_T (and the derived products alpha-bar) that sets how fast the forward process destroys the signal.
Denoiser
The neural network that receives a noisy sample and its timestep and predicts the noise that was added (or the clean sample).
Timestep (t)
The index of the noise level; the denoiser is told t so one set of weights can handle every level from slightly noisy to pure noise.
U-Net
A convolutional network that shrinks an image through several resolutions and expands it again, with skip connections that carry fine detail across.
Diffusion transformer (DiT)
A denoiser that cuts the noisy array into patches, treats each patch as a token and processes the tokens with transformer blocks.
Latent diffusion
Running the diffusion process on the compressed latent array of a pretrained autoencoder instead of on pixels, then decoding the result.
Classifier-free guidance
A sampling rule that extrapolates from the unconditional noise prediction towards the prompt-conditioned one to make the output follow the prompt more closely.
Scheduler (sampler)
The code that turns the denoiser's prediction into the next, less noisy sample and decides which timesteps to visit.

2Explanation

Introduction

You have met the ingredients already. An autoencoder compresses data to a small code and decodes it back, a generative model samples new data from a learned distribution, and an attention layer lets one set of vectors read from another. A diffusion model adds one more idea: destroying data is easy to simulate, so learn to reverse the destruction.

Take a photograph and add a little random static, as on a badly tuned television. Do it again, a thousand times in all, and the picture is gone. This is the forward process, and it needs no learning; it is a fixed recipe. Now suppose a network could look at a slightly noisy picture, be told how noisy it is, and predict the noise that was added. Subtracting that prediction gives a slightly cleaner picture. Start from pure static, repeat this many times, and a picture appears that was never in the training set. That repeated cleaning is the reverse process, and running it is called sampling.

Two details make this practical. Training never runs the thousand-step chain: a closed-form formula jumps straight to any noise level, so each training example costs one network call at a randomly chosen level. And the network is told the level, the timestep ttt, so one set of weights covers everything from "barely noisy" to "pure static".

The lesson covers the maths of both processes, the training objective, the two common denoiser designs (U-Nets and transformers), why Stable Diffusion-style systems work on a compressed latent image, how a text prompt and guidance steer the result, and why the number of sampling steps is the main trade between speed and quality. A worked example with four numbers can be reproduced in a few lines of standard-library Python.

How it works

The forward process: noise on a schedule

Let x0x_0x0​ be a clean sample, for example an image with pixel values scaled to [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]. The forward process builds x1,x2,…,xTx_1, x_2, \dots, x_Tx1​,x2​,…,xT​ by adding a little Gaussian noise at each step:

xt=1−βt xt−1+βt εt,εt∼N(0,I)x_t = \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\,\varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)xt​=1−βt​​xt−1​+βt​​εt​,εt​∼N(0,I)

The numbers β1,…,βT\beta_1, \dots, \beta_Tβ1​,…,βT​ are the noise schedule. The original DDPM paper uses T=1000T = 1000T=1000 with βt\beta_tβt​ rising linearly from 10−410^{-4}10−4 to 0.020.020.02 (Ho et al., 2020 (opens in a new tab)). Write αt=1−βt\alpha_t = 1-\beta_tαt​=1−βt​ and αˉt=α1α2⋯αt\bar\alpha_t = \alpha_1\alpha_2\cdots\alpha_tαˉt​=α1​α2​⋯αt​. A sum of Gaussians is Gaussian, so the whole chain collapses into one formula that reaches any step directly:

xt=αˉt x0+1−αˉt ε,ε∼N(0,I)x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)xt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ε,ε∼N(0,I)

Read it as a blend of signal and noise. αˉt\bar\alpha_tαˉt​ starts at 1 and falls towards 0, so early steps keep most of the picture and late steps keep almost none.

The linear schedule is a choice, not a law. Nichol and Dhariwal (opens in a new tab) found it sub-optimal for 64×64 and 32×32 images: the end of the forward process is so noisy that it adds little to sample quality. Their cosine schedule, αˉt=f(t)/f(0)\bar\alpha_t = f(t)/f(0)αˉt​=f(t)/f(0) with f(t)=cos⁡2 ⁣(t/T+s1+s⋅π2)f(t)=\cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{t/T+s}{1+s}\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2}\big)f(t)=cos2(1+st/T+s​⋅2π​) and s=0.008s=0.008s=0.008, declines more gently, as the plot shows.

The training objective: predict the noise

Training draws a clean sample from the data set, a random level ttt and a fresh noise draw ε\varepsilonε, builds xtx_txt​ with the closed form, and asks the network εθ(xt,t)\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)εθ​(xt​,t) to guess ε\varepsilonε:

Lsimple=Ex0, t, ε[ ∥ε−εθ(αˉt x0+1−αˉt ε,  t)∥2]L_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\,t,\,\varepsilon}\Big[\,\big\lVert \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon,\; t\big)\big\rVert^2\Big]Lsimple​=Ex0​,t,ε​[​ε−εθ​(αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ε,t)​2]

This is ordinary regression with a target we made ourselves. DDPM derives it from a variational bound and finds that dropping the bound's per-step weights works best, hence "simplified". Predicting the noise is interchangeable with predicting the clean sample, because x^0=(xt−1−αˉt ε^)/αˉt\hat{x}_0 = (x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat\varepsilon)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x^0​=(xt​−1−αˉt​​ε^)/αˉt​​; some systems predict x0x_0x0​ directly.

python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def training_step(model, x0, alpha_bar):
    """x0: batch of images in [-1, 1]; alpha_bar: tensor on the same device, alpha_bar[i] is the product for timestep i + 1."""
    t = torch.randint(0, len(alpha_bar), (x0.shape[0],), device=x0.device)   # one random level per example
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    a = alpha_bar[t].view(-1, 1, 1, 1)
    x_t = a.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - a).sqrt() * eps                 # closed-form forward jump
    return F.mse_loss(model(x_t, t), eps)                      # compare the guess with the true noise

The reverse process: sampling

To generate, start from xT∼N(0,I)x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)xT​∼N(0,I) and for t=T,…,1t = T, \dots, 1t=T,…,1 compute

xt−1=1αt(xt−1−αt1−αˉt εθ(xt,t))+σtz,z∼N(0,I)x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{1-\alpha_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\Big) + \sigma_t z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)xt−1​=αt​​1​(xt​−1−αˉt​​1−αt​​εθ​(xt​,t))+σt​z,z∼N(0,I)

with z=0z = 0z=0 on the last step. The bracket removes a scaled copy of the predicted noise, the factor in front undoes the shrinking by αt\sqrt{\alpha_t}αt​​ that the forward step applied, and σtz\sigma_t zσt​z adds a small fresh kick so that different runs diverge. Each step changes the sample only slightly, which is why the original sampler needs a thousand network calls per image.

Denoiser networks: U-Nets and transformers

The denoiser maps a noisy array and a timestep to an array of the same shape. DDPM used a U-Net with group normalisation, self-attention at 16×16 resolution and a sinusoidal timestep embedding added into every residual block. The Stable Diffusion pipeline documented by Hugging Face (opens in a new tab) still uses a U-Net, with 860 million parameters.

Diffusion transformers (DiT) instead cut the latent into p×pp \times pp×p patches, treat each patch as a token and apply transformer blocks. Peebles and Xie (opens in a new tab) compared ways of feeding in the timestep and class, and found an adaptive layer norm variant (adaLN-Zero) gave lower FID than cross-attention or in-context tokens. FID (Fréchet inception distance) scores how far generated images are from real ones, and lower is better. They report a strong negative correlation between forward-pass Gflops (billions of floating-point operations) and FID, and their largest model reached FID 2.27 on 256×256 ImageNet with guidance. Stable Diffusion 3 uses a related multimodal design that keeps separate weights for text tokens and image tokens (opens in a new tab). DiT keeps the DDPM noise-prediction loss, so swapping the U-Net for a transformer does not by itself change the objective. Stable Diffusion 3 changes more than the network: its research post says it uses a rectified-flow formulation, in which data and noise are connected along a linear trajectory, instead of the DDPM schedule above.

Latent diffusion: denoise a compressed picture

A 512×512 RGB image has 786,432 values, and running a large denoiser on that array dozens of times is costly; the latent diffusion paper (opens in a new tab) notes that training the strongest pixel-space models often takes hundreds of GPU days. Its remedy is to train an autoencoder first, then run the whole diffusion process on the encoder's output zzz with the same loss:

LLDM=EE(x), ε, t[∥ε−εθ(zt,t)∥2]L_{\text{LDM}} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{E}(x),\,\varepsilon,\,t}\Big[\big\lVert \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(z_t, t)\big\rVert^2\Big]LLDM​=EE(x),ε,t​[​ε−εθ​(zt​,t)​2]

Of the downsampling factors they compared, 4 and 8 gave the best conditions for high-quality synthesis. The Stable Diffusion pipeline uses a factor of 8, so the initial noise has one eighth of the image height and width, and the final latent is decoded by the VAE (variational autoencoder) decoder. The DiT paper reports that this VAE turns a 256×256×3 image into a 32×32×4 latent, which means a 512×512 image becomes 64×64×4, or 16,384 values: 48 times fewer than the 786,432 pixel values.

Text conditioning and classifier-free guidance

A prompt reaches the denoiser in two stages. A text encoder turns it into a sequence of embedding vectors: a frozen CLIP text encoder (trained alongside an image encoder to match captions with images) in Stable Diffusion, and a frozen T5 language model in Imagen (opens in a new tab), whose authors found that enlarging the text encoder helped more than enlarging the image model. The vectors then enter the denoiser through cross-attention, softmax⁡(QK⊤/d) V\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})\,Vsoftmax(QK⊤/d​)V, with queries from image features and keys and values from the text embeddings.

Conditioning alone follows prompts loosely. Classifier-free guidance tightens it. In training the prompt is replaced by an empty one some of the time (Dieleman reports that 10 to 20 percent tends to work well (opens in a new tab)), so one network learns both conditional and unconditional predictions. At each sampling step both are computed and extrapolated:

ε~=εθ(xt,∅)+s (εθ(xt,c)−εθ(xt,∅))\tilde\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) + s\,\big(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, c) - \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing)\big)ε~=εθ​(xt​,∅)+s(εθ​(xt​,c)−εθ​(xt​,∅))

Here ccc is the prompt embedding, ∅\varnothing∅ the empty-prompt embedding and sss the guidance scale. With s=1s = 1s=1 you get plain conditional sampling. Ho and Salimans (opens in a new tab) write the same rule with weight w=s−1w = s - 1w=s−1, and show that raising it lowers sample variety and raises individual fidelity. The Diffusers documentation (opens in a new tab) gives guidance_scale a default of 7.5 and warns that higher values trade image quality for prompt adherence. Imagen reports that large weights give saturated, unnatural images and adds dynamic thresholding to counter it. The price is two network evaluations per step.

Sampling steps and the quality trade

Each step is one denoiser call, so latency scales with the step count (doubled by guidance). DDIM showed that the same trained network can be sampled along a short subsequence of timesteps, with a generalised update

xτi−1=αˉτi−1 x^0+1−αˉτi−1−σ2 ε^+σzx_{\tau_{i-1}} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{\tau_{i-1}}}\,\hat{x}_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{\tau_{i-1}}-\sigma^2}\,\hat\varepsilon + \sigma zxτi−1​​=αˉτi−1​​​x^0​+1−αˉτi−1​​−σ2​ε^+σz

where x^0\hat{x}_0x^0​ and ε^\hat\varepsilonε^ come from the network at timestep τi\tau_iτi​, and σ\sigmaσ is set by a parameter η\etaη. With η=0\eta = 0η=0 the noise term vanishes and sampling is deterministic. The authors report 10 to 50 times faster sampling, and the bar chart shows the cost: with only 10 steps the CIFAR-10 FID is 13.36 for the deterministic sampler and 41.07 for the fully stochastic one, against 4.04 and 4.73 respectively with 1000 steps.

Other levers exist: learned variances let a model sample in as few as 50 passes with little loss; better solvers and timestep spacing (the Diffusers scheduler guide (opens in a new tab) shows a 10-step schedule) produce good images with far fewer steps; and distillation trains a student to give good samples in one to four steps. Each lever either reduces discretisation error or moves the work into training, and none removes the trade entirely.

Worked example: Noising, scoring and denoising a four-pixel image at t = 250

We use the DDPM schedule from the lesson (T=1000T = 1000T=1000, βt\beta_tβt​ rising linearly from 10−410^{-4}10−4 to 0.020.020.02) and a four-pixel "image" with values in [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]. The script at the end reproduces every number.

Training adjusts the weights to shrink this number, averaged over many images, levels and noise draws.

Rearranging the closed form gives x^0=(xt−0.6899 ε^)/0.7239\hat{x}_0 = (x_t - 0.6899\,\hat\varepsilon)/0.7239x^0​=(xt​−0.6899ε^)/0.7239, which here is [0.8953,−0.5906,0.0094,−0.8094][0.8953, -0.5906, 0.0094, -0.8094][0.8953,−0.5906,0.0094,−0.8094]. Step 4: one reverse step. With σt=βt=0.0711\sigma_t = \sqrt{\beta_t} = 0.0711σt​=βt​​=0.0711 and the fresh noise z=[0.3,−0.5,1.1,0.2]z = [0.3, -0.5, 1.1, 0.2]z=[0.3,−0.5,1.1,0.2], the update from the lesson gives a mean of [0.9235,−1.1129,0.3490,−0.1085][0.9235, -1.1129, 0.3490, -0.1085][0.9235,−1.1129,0.3490,−0.1085] and x249=[0.9448,−1.1485,0.4272,−0.0942]x_{249} = [0.9448, -1.1485, 0.4272, -0.0942]x249​=[0.9448,−1.1485,0.4272,−0.0942]. python
import math

T = 1000
betas = [1e-4 + (0.02 - 1e-4) * i / (T - 1) for i in range(T)]   # beta_1 .. beta_T
alpha_bar, running = [], 1.0
for b in betas:
    running *= 1 - b
    alpha_bar.append(running)                                    # alpha_bar[t - 1] is the value for step t

t = 250
beta, alpha, abar = betas[t - 1], 1 - betas[t - 1], alpha_bar[t - 1]
sa, sn = math.sqrt(abar), math.sqrt(1 - abar)
print(f"beta={beta:.5f} alpha={alpha:.5f} abar={abar:.4f} sqrt(abar)={sa:.4f} sqrt(1-abar)={sn:.4f}")

x0 = [0.8, -0.4, 0.2, -1.0]
eps = [0.5, -1.2, 0.3, 0.9]
xt = [sa * a + sn * e for a, e in zip(x0, eps)]
print("x_t     ", [round(v, 4) for v in xt])

eps_hat = [0.4, -1.0, 0.5, 0.7]
loss = sum((e - h) ** 2 for e, h in zip(eps, eps_hat)) / len(eps)
print("loss    ", round(loss, 4))

x0_hat = [(x - sn * h) / sa for x, h in zip(xt, eps_hat)]
print("x0_hat  ", [round(v, 4) for v in x0_hat])

mean = [(x - (1 - alpha) / sn * h) / math.sqrt(alpha) for x, h in zip(xt, eps_hat)]
sigma, z = math.sqrt(beta), [0.3, -0.5, 1.1, 0.2]
x_prev = [m + sigma * zz for m, zz in zip(mean, z)]
print("mean    ", [round(v, 4) for v in mean])
print("x_{t-1} ", [round(v, 4) for v in x_prev])

Edge cases and limitations

High guidance scales saturate and narrow the output
Raising the guidance scale pushes the sample harder towards the prompt, and past a point it hurts. Ho and Salimans show variety falling as guidance rises. Imagen's authors report saturated, unnatural images at large weights, because predictions leave the range seen in training, and add dynamic thresholding to counter it. The Diffusers documentation warns that higher values lower image quality. Sweep the scale with a fixed seed and stop when colours burn out or the images start to look alike.
A scheduler must match the checkpoint it drives
A scheduler holds configuration, not weights, but that configuration encodes the number of training timesteps and the noise setup the network was trained with. The Diffusers guide says to swap schedulers with from_config() on the existing scheduler config so that num_train_timesteps and related fields stay aligned, and to keep the default FlowMatch scheduler for flow-matching checkpoints such as Flux unless you are experimenting on purpose. A mismatch typically shows up as degraded images, not as an error message.
The autoencoder sets a ceiling on pixel-level detail
In a latent model every image passes through the decoder, so no amount of denoising adds detail the decoder cannot reproduce. The latent diffusion authors note that reconstruction can become a bottleneck for tasks needing fine-grained accuracy in pixel space. To see the best case, encode and decode a real image with the VAE alone and compare it with the original before blaming the diffusion step.
Cutting steps works only to a point and needs the right sampler
With a fixed trained network, fewer steps mean larger discretisation errors. In the DDIM paper's CIFAR-10 results the stochastic sampler's FID is 41.07 at 10 steps against 4.73 at 1000, while the deterministic sampler goes from 13.36 to 4.04. The Diffusers guide notes that trailing timestep spacing typically helps at low step counts, and it lists TCDScheduler as working well for distilled models and LCMScheduler for few-step generation with an LCM checkpoint. Going down to one to four steps generally calls for a model distilled for that purpose, such as SDXL-Turbo. In the first exercise the error is negligible at 20 steps and large at 5.
Patch size and resolution drive a transformer denoiser's cost
A diffusion transformer sees (I/p)² tokens for latent side I and patch size p. In the DiT paper, a smaller patch size means more tokens and more forward-pass Gflops, and Gflops rather than parameter count tracked FID. Doubling a latent's side length likewise quadruples the tokens, so memory and latency grow quickly with output resolution.

When to use it, and when something simpler is enough

Use it when

  • You need varied, high-fidelity samples of images, video or other continuous data and can afford tens of denoiser calls per sample, or can use a model distilled to a few steps.
  • You want to steer generation with a conditioning signal such as text, a class, a motif or the previous weather state, which enters the denoiser as extra input.
  • You need many plausible outputs for one input, as in an ensemble forecast, rather than a single best guess.
  • You prefer a plain regression training loss over the adversarial game a GAN requires.

Think twice when

  • Latency must be a few milliseconds per sample and no distilled model exists for your domain; a GAN or a decoder-only network samples in one pass.
  • The task has one correct answer to be predicted or classified; a discriminative model is cheaper and gives a verifiable output.

A simpler alternative. If you only need to classify, regress or retrieve, use a discriminative model, which needs one forward pass and no sampling. If you need quick samples from a small, low-dimensional distribution, a VAE or a GAN is often enough. Reach for diffusion when sample quality, diversity and conditioning control matter more than sampling speed, and budget the step count explicitly.

Key takeaways

  • A diffusion model is trained to predict the noise added to a sample at a random noise level, and it generates by starting from pure noise and removing predicted noise in many small steps.
  • The closed form x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) noise lets training jump to any level in one step, and the noise schedule that sets alpha-bar decides how quickly information is destroyed.
  • Latent diffusion runs the denoiser on a compressed latent from an autoencoder, which makes high-resolution generation affordable and makes the decoder the ceiling on pixel-level detail.
  • Text enters through cross-attention or joint attention, and classifier-free guidance extrapolates from the unconditional to the conditional prediction, so a higher scale follows the prompt more closely, reduces variety and doubles the work per step.
  • The number of sampling steps is the main speed and quality dial, because each step is one denoiser call, and deterministic samplers, better solvers and distillation lower the count at some cost in quality.
  • U-Nets and transformers are both used as denoisers, and swapping one for the other, as in DiT, leaves the noise-prediction objective unchanged, although some transformer-based systems such as Stable Diffusion 3 also change the noising path to rectified flow.

Sources for this explanation: [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [11], [12]

3Real-world applications

5 documented uses of Diffusion Models. Each one names the real system, the problem it solves and its tradeoff, with links to the sources.

  1. Stable Diffusion: text-to-image generation in a latent space on consumer GPUs
  2. Stable Video Diffusion: adding temporal layers to an image diffusion model
  3. GenCast: sampling 15-day weather ensembles with a conditional diffusion model
  4. RFdiffusion: designing protein backbones by denoising residue frames
  5. SDXL-Turbo: adversarial diffusion distillation for one-step image generation

Example 1 of 5

Stable Diffusion: text-to-image generation in a latent space on consumer GPUs

Stable Diffusion (CompVis, Stability AI, Runway, LAION)Documented in official docs

The Hugging Face Diffusers documentation describes the Stable Diffusion text-to-image pipeline, a latent diffusion model created by CompVis, Stability AI, Runway and LAION, and its tutorial "Understanding pipelines, models and schedulers" lists the full denoising loop. The method itself is in the latent diffusion paper. [5][13][11][6]

The problem

Diffusion models that denoise raw pixels are expensive. The latent diffusion paper states that training the most powerful ones often takes hundreds of GPU days, and sampling is slow because it needs many sequential network evaluations. The practical aim was a text-to-image model that keeps the quality and flexibility of diffusion, follows a text prompt, trains on limited compute and runs on a single consumer GPU.

Where this topic fits

The diffusion process runs on a latent array one eighth the height and width of the image, not on pixels. Before it, a tokenizer and a frozen text encoder turn the prompt and an empty prompt into embeddings. During it, a U-Net denoises the latent once per scheduler timestep, reading the embeddings through cross-attention, and the guidance rule combines its conditional and unconditional predictions. After it, the VAE decoder turns the final latent into the image.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Tokenise the prompt and encode it with the frozen CLIP text encoder. Encode an empty prompt as well, to serve as the unconditional input for guidance.
  2. Draw Gaussian noise with the latent shape (channels, height divided by 8, width divided by 8) from a seeded generator so the run is repeatable.
  3. Ask the scheduler for its timesteps (the tutorial uses 25, the pipeline default is 50) and multiply the noise by the scheduler's initial noise scale.
  4. At each timestep run the U-Net on the unconditional and conditional inputs together, split the two noise predictions and combine them with the guidance scale.
  5. Hand the guided prediction to the scheduler, which returns the latent for the previous timestep, and repeat until the timesteps run out.
  6. Divide the final latent by 0.18215 (the scaling factor of the VAE used in the tutorial), decode it with the VAE and rescale the output from [-1, 1] to 0 to 255 pixel values to obtain the image.

Why this approach fits

Pixel-space denoising at 512×512 would process 786,432 values per network call. The latent is 64×64×4 = 16,384 values if the VAE uses four latent channels, as the DiT paper reports for the Stable Diffusion autoencoder, a 48-fold reduction (our arithmetic). Because the repeated loop runs on that small array, the 860-million-parameter U-Net is light enough for consumer GPUs, which is how the documentation describes the model. Cross-attention gives the denoiser a place to read the prompt, and guidance gets prompt adherence without training a separate classifier.

Limitation or tradeoff

Quality is bounded by the autoencoder, which the paper names as a possible bottleneck for tasks that need fine pixel accuracy. Sampling is still sequential, and the authors acknowledge it is slower than a GAN. Guidance makes each step cost two U-Net evaluations, and the documentation says that raising the guidance scale improves prompt adherence at the expense of image quality, so the default of 7.5 is a compromise rather than a free setting.

What the sources document

  • The Diffusers documentation describes Stable Diffusion as a text-to-image latent diffusion model created by researchers and engineers from CompVis, Stability AI, Runway and LAION, trained on 512×512 images from a subset of LAION-5B, conditioned with a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder, and light enough (860M-parameter UNet, 123M text encoder) to run on consumer GPUs. [13]
  • The latent diffusion paper says training the strongest pixel-space diffusion models often takes hundreds of GPU days, that diffusion in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder lowers the cost, and that cross-attention layers let inputs such as text condition generation; it also concedes that sampling is slower than a GAN's and that reconstruction can limit fine pixel accuracy. [5]
  • The Diffusers tutorial builds the pipeline from a VAE, a CLIP text encoder, a UNet and a scheduler: it starts from latent noise whose height and width are divided by 8, calls the UNet with the text embeddings, combines the unconditional and text predictions with the guidance scale, steps the scheduler, and finally divides the latents by 0.18215 before VAE decoding. [11]
  • The pipeline reference lists num_inference_steps with a default of 50, where more steps usually give higher quality at the expense of slower inference, and guidance_scale with a default of 7.5, where a higher value ties images more closely to the prompt at the expense of lower image quality. [13]
  • The DiT paper uses the off-the-shelf pretrained VAE from Stable Diffusion, which downsamples by 8 and turns a 256×256×3 image into a 32×32×4 latent. [6]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 2 of 5

Stable Video Diffusion: adding temporal layers to an image diffusion model

Documented in a paper

The Stable Video Diffusion paper (Blattmann et al.) describes a latent video diffusion model for text-to-video and image-to-video generation, built by extending the Stable Diffusion 2.1 image model and training it on a curated video dataset. [14]

The problem

Image diffusion models are strong, but video needs consistency across frames, and raw video collections are messy: they contain cuts, nearly static clips, overlaid text and poor captions. The paper asks how to turn an image diffusion model into a video model and which data and training stages make that work. It argues that the distribution of the training data has a large influence on a generative model.

Where this topic fits

Diffusion runs on latents for a short stack of video frames instead of one image, with the same noising and denoising objective as in this lesson. What changes is the denoiser, which gains layers that look across frames, and the training pipeline, which curates the video data and trains in stages.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Start from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model, Stable Diffusion 2.1 (stage I, image pretraining), so the network already knows how to denoise single frames.
  2. Insert temporal convolution and attention layers after every spatial convolution and attention layer, so features can also mix along the frame axis.
  3. Curate a large video collection by detecting cuts, removing static clips with optical flow, scoring aesthetics with CLIP embeddings, filtering text-heavy clips with OCR and adding synthetic captions.
  4. Stage II is video pretraining on the curated collection at low resolution.
  5. Stage III is fine-tuning on a smaller set of high-quality videos at higher resolution.
  6. Sample like any latent diffusion model: in a typical implementation, start from noise for every frame of a clip and denoise the frames together, conditioned on a text prompt or a starting image.

Why this approach fits

Video is image data with an extra axis, and the denoising objective does not care what shape the array has. Reusing a pretrained image model keeps its knowledge of appearance and lets the new layers concentrate on motion. Running diffusion on latents keeps the cost of a whole clip manageable, for the same reason as for a single image.

Limitation or tradeoff

More frames and higher resolution multiply the cost. The paper's base model produces 14 frames at 320×576, so clips are short and low resolution. The result also depends on the data pipeline: the authors stress that the training data distribution has a large impact, so the filtering and captioning stages are part of the method rather than preparation that can be skipped.

What the sources document

  • Stable Video Diffusion is described as a latent video diffusion model for text-to-video and image-to-video generation, trained in three stages: image pretraining grounded in Stable Diffusion 2.1, video pretraining on a large curated video dataset, and fine-tuning on smaller high-quality video at higher resolution. [14]
  • The 2D image model is extended by inserting temporal convolution and attention layers after every spatial convolution and attention layer. [14]
  • The paper's text says the Large Video Dataset starts with 580 million annotated video clips covering 212 years of content (its Table 1 lists 577 million clips), and that the filtered training set has 152 million examples. [14]
  • Curation uses cascaded cut detection, optical-flow filtering of static scenes, aesthetic scoring with CLIP embeddings, OCR filtering of text-heavy clips and synthetic captioning. [14]
  • The base model generates 14 frames at 320×576 resolution, and the authors state that pretraining on a large diverse dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller higher-quality one significantly improves performance. [14]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 3 of 5

GenCast: sampling 15-day weather ensembles with a conditional diffusion model

Google DeepMindDocumented in an engineering article

Google DeepMind's GenCast paper and its announcement post describe a conditional diffusion model that forecasts global weather. Each sampled forecast is one possible weather trajectory, and an ensemble is built by drawing many such trajectories from different noise. [16][15]

The problem

Weather is uncertain, so forecasters want a spread of plausible futures rather than one prediction, in order to estimate how likely extremes such as heat, high winds or a tropical cyclone track are. The operational benchmark, ECMWF's ENS, is itself an ensemble forecast. The question is whether a learned model can generate a probability distribution over future weather that beats it, at global 0.25° resolution out to 15 days.

Where this topic fits

The thing being generated is the next 12-hour atmospheric state on a global grid. The diffusion model is a conditional generator: given the two most recent states, it turns a noise field into the next state. The rollout repeats this 30 times, and each different noise draw yields a different ensemble member.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Take the two most recent atmospheric states as conditioning input for the denoiser; the noise level is also given to it.
  2. Draw a fresh Gaussian noise field over the global grid.
  3. Run the denoiser for 20 solver steps with a second-order solver, which needs 39 denoiser evaluations in total, to turn the noise into the state 12 hours ahead.
  4. Append that state and repeat, 30 times, to reach 15 days. Errors from early steps carry forward because each step conditions on the previous ones.
  5. Repeat the whole rollout with different noise to produce more members, which the blog says can run in parallel, and evaluate the 50-member ensembles against ENS.

Why this approach fits

Weather forecasting needs a distribution, and a diffusion model is a sampler for a learned distribution: changing the noise gives a different, equally plausible future, so an ensemble is simply many samples. The conditioning on recent states plays the role the text prompt plays for images.

Limitation or tradeoff

Every member is a full rollout of 1,170 denoiser evaluations, so ensemble size is a compute decision, and the quoted 8 minutes is for one forecast on one TPU, with members run in parallel on more hardware. The skill figures are specific to the evaluation protocol of 1,320 variable, lead-time and level combinations against ENS, not a general guarantee for every region or event. The percentage also depends on the version of the work: the announcement gives 97.2%, while the abstract of the arXiv preprint cited here (version 2) reports 97.4% of 1,320 targets.

What the sources document

  • Google DeepMind describes GenCast as a diffusion model adapted to Earth's spherical geometry, whose forecast is an ensemble of 50 or more predictions, each a possible weather trajectory, at 0.25° resolution up to 15 days ahead, trained on four decades of ERA5 data. [16]
  • A single Google Cloud TPU v5 takes about 8 minutes to produce one 15-day forecast in the ensemble, and every forecast in the ensemble can be generated simultaneously, in parallel. [16]
  • The paper conditions the denoiser on the previous two atmospheric states, uses 12-hour steps so that T = 30 covers 15 days, takes 20 solver steps per forecast step with a second-order solver, and counts 39 function evaluations of the denoiser per forecast step. [15]
  • The announcement reports that GenCast was more accurate than ENS on 97.2% of the 1,320 evaluated targets and on 99.8% at lead times greater than 36 hours. [16]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 4 of 5

RFdiffusion: designing protein backbones by denoising residue frames

University of Washington Institute for Protein Design (code: RosettaCommons)Documented in a paper

The Nature paper "De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion" (read through its open full text on PubMed Central) and the RFdiffusion repository README describe a diffusion model that generates protein backbones, built by fine-tuning the RoseTTAFold structure prediction network. [17][18]

The problem

Designing a protein that folds into a chosen shape, binds a chosen target or holds a functional motif in place means searching an enormous space of 3D backbones. The task is to generate new backbones, optionally constrained by a motif, a binding target or a symmetry, which can then be turned into sequences and tested in the laboratory.

Where this topic fits

The data being noised and denoised is a set of residue frames rather than pixels. The network predicts the clean structure at each step, and conditioning inputs such as motif coordinates and target hotspot residues steer the trajectory. The generated backbone is the start of a design pipeline whose output is judged by experiment.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Represent every residue as a frame: a Cα coordinate plus an N-Cα-C orientation.
  2. Define a noising process that fits the data's geometry: 3D Gaussian noise on the coordinates and Brownian motion on the manifold of rotation matrices for the orientations.
  3. Fine-tune RoseTTAFold to take a noised structure and a timestep and predict the denoised structure, with a mean squared error loss between predicted and true frames.
  4. Add self-conditioning, so the model can read its own previous prediction between timesteps.
  5. Supply design constraints as input: motif coordinates, interface hotspot residues on a target, or a point-group symmetry.
  6. Generate by starting from random frames and denoising, then test selected designs experimentally.

Why this approach fits

Protein design needs many different outputs that satisfy the same constraints, which a stochastic sampler provides. Defining the noise on the data's own geometry (positions and rotations) lets the same denoise-and- repeat recipe work on structured scientific data, and feeding constraints as conditioning avoids retraining for each design problem. Predicting the clean structure rather than the noise is a design choice; for plain Euclidean data the two are linked by the identity in the lesson.

Limitation or tradeoff

Generation is only the first stage. The paper reports an overall experimental binder success rate of 19% across five targets, so most designs did not reach the binding threshold, although the authors call it a conservative estimate. Training noised structures for up to 200 steps, and the README describes lowering the inference default to 50 and says about 20 steps often gives equivalent in silico quality, which is another case of trading steps for cost.

What the sources document

  • RFdiffusion is built by fine-tuning the RoseTTAFold structure prediction network on protein structure denoising tasks, and the paper reports that fine-tuning from pretrained weights was far more successful than training for an equivalent time from untrained weights. [17]
  • Each residue is a frame with a Cα coordinate and an N-Cα-C orientation. Coordinates are perturbed with 3D Gaussian noise, orientations with Brownian motion on the manifold of rotation matrices, and the network predicts the denoised structure directly, trained with mean squared error between predicted and true frames. [17]
  • The paper generates training inputs by noising structures for up to 200 steps, with typical trajectories of 200 steps, and reports that self-conditioning improved in silico performance; the README says the model was originally trained with 200 discrete timesteps, the inference default is now 50, and in many cases about 20 steps gives outputs of equivalent in silico quality to 200 steps. [17][18]
  • Conditioning uses motifs given as 3D coordinates, interface hotspot residues on the target chain for binder design, and point-group symmetry for oligomers; the README lists motif scaffolding, unconditional and symmetric generation, binder design and partial diffusion. [17][18]
  • Across five targets, with fewer than 100 designs tested per target, the overall experimental binder success rate (binding at or above 50% of the positive control's maximal response) was 19%, and a cryo-EM structure of the binder HA_20 with influenza haemagglutinin, at 2.9 Å, closely matched its design model. [17]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 5 of 5

SDXL-Turbo: adversarial diffusion distillation for one-step image generation

Stability AIDocumented in an open-source project

The Hugging Face model card for stabilityai/sdxl-turbo and the Adversarial Diffusion Distillation paper describe a distilled version of SDXL 1.0 that generates images in one to four steps. The Diffusers scheduler guide documents the scheduler side of few-step sampling. [20][19][12]

The problem

A standard text-to-image diffusion model needs tens of denoiser calls per image; the Diffusers Stable Diffusion pipeline defaults to 50 steps. That is too slow for interactive, real-time use. The ADD paper notes that GANs are fast but lower in quality, and sets out to keep diffusion-level quality with sampling in one to four steps.

Where this topic fits

The step count is the thing being cut. A student network is trained once, starting from a pretrained diffusion model. At inference the student replaces the teacher in the same denoise loop but runs it one to four times, and the example on the model card turns guidance off.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Start the student from the weights of a pretrained diffusion model, SDXL.
  2. Train with an adversarial loss: a discriminator pushes the student's few-step outputs towards the distribution of real images.
  3. Add a distillation loss from a frozen teacher diffusion model so the student keeps the teacher's composition and text alignment.
  4. At inference run the student for one to four steps. The model card example uses a single step.
  5. Set guidance_scale to 0.0 as the card does, so the extra unconditional pass that guidance would add disappears.

Why this approach fits

The cost of a diffusion sample is steps times evaluations per step. A Stable Diffusion pipeline at its documented defaults runs 50 steps with guidance, which is 100 U-Net evaluations. The Turbo card's example runs one step with guidance off, which is one evaluation, so distillation attacks both factors at once (this counts evaluations, not seconds, because the networks differ in size). Starting the student from pretrained diffusion weights reuses what the teacher learned instead of building a one-step generator from scratch.

Limitation or tradeoff

The model card lists a fixed 512×512 output, imperfect photorealism, no legible text and faces or people that may be generated poorly. The paper's quality claims come from its authors' human preference studies and COCO metrics, not from independent tests. With one to four steps there is also less room to refine an image by iteration, and with guidance off the usual guidance-scale control over prompt adherence is not used.

What the sources document

  • The model card calls SDXL-Turbo a distilled version of SDXL 1.0 trained for real-time synthesis, built with Adversarial Diffusion Distillation to sample in 1 to 4 steps, and its example sets num_inference_steps to 1 and guidance_scale to 0.0. [20]
  • The card lists limitations: generated images have a fixed resolution of 512×512, the model does not achieve perfect photorealism, it cannot render legible text, and faces and people may not be generated properly. [20]
  • The ADD paper trains a student initialised from a pretrained diffusion model with an adversarial loss from a discriminator plus a score distillation loss from a frozen teacher diffusion model. [19]
  • In its own user studies the paper reports that ADD-XL with one step outperforms LCM-XL at four steps and that with four steps it beats SDXL-Base at 50 steps in the majority of comparisons, and it claims to be the first method to unlock single-step, real-time image synthesis with foundation models. [19]
  • The Diffusers scheduler guide says schedulers trade speed for quality, lists LCMScheduler for few-step generation and TCDScheduler for distilled models, and shows an Align Your Steps schedule that it says can produce a high-quality image in 10 steps. [12]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

4Common mistakes

  1. Swapping in a scheduler or a step count without matching the checkpoint's configuration

    Why it causes problems
    The network was trained for a particular noise schedule and parameterisation. A scheduler built with different settings feeds it noise levels it was not trained on, so images come out noisy, washed out or distorted, and no exception is raised.
    How to recognise it
    Images look wrong only after you change the scheduler, while the same prompt and seed look fine with the checkpoint's default scheduler.
    How to fix it
    Build the new scheduler with from_config(pipeline.scheduler.config), as the Diffusers guide advises, keep flow-matching checkpoints on their default FlowMatch scheduler unless you are deliberately experimenting, and compare against the default at the same seed.

  2. Raising the guidance scale to fix weak prompt following

    Why it causes problems
    Past a point, higher guidance saturates colours, flattens detail and makes different seeds look alike. You swap one defect for another and still pay for two network passes per step.
    How to recognise it
    Over-contrasted, burnt or near-duplicate images across seeds as the scale rises. A grid of scales at one seed shows where quality turns.
    How to fix it
    Sweep the scale around the checkpoint default (7.5 in the Diffusers Stable Diffusion pipeline) with a fixed seed, stop at the first sign of saturation, and improve the prompt or the model if adherence is still weak.

  3. Judging step counts or samplers from a single seed

    Why it causes problems
    The starting noise changes the image more than most settings do, so one picture says little about a setting. You may keep a worse configuration because one seed happened to look better.
    How to recognise it
    The ranking of two configurations flips when you change the seed.
    How to fix it
    Fix the seed with a torch.Generator to compare settings on identical starting noise, then confirm on many seeds with a metric or a blind human comparison before choosing.

  4. Counting sampling steps and forgetting that guidance doubles the evaluations

    Why it causes problems
    Latency and GPU cost estimates come out at roughly half of reality, and the gain from a distilled model that turns guidance off is misjudged, so a budget based on steps alone is wrong.
    How to recognise it
    Measured latency is about twice the step count times the single-pass time, and profiling shows the batch dimension doubled in the denoiser call.
    How to fix it
    Budget evaluations as steps times passes per step. In Diffusers a guidance_scale above 1 means two passes, batched together, and a distilled model that sets the scale to 0.0 needs one.

  5. Hand-writing a latent pipeline and forgetting the latent scaling or the value range

    Why it causes problems
    The VAE decoder expects latents at a particular scale, and the final conversion assumes pixel values in [-1, 1]. Omit the 1/0.18215 rescale or the (image / 2 + 0.5) mapping and the output is garbled, saturated or clipped even though the loop ran without errors.
    How to recognise it
    Blown-out, uniformly grey or noise-like images. Printing the minimum and maximum of the decoded tensor shows values far outside [-1, 1].
    How to fix it
    Follow the order in the Diffusers tutorial: scale the initial noise by the scheduler's init_noise_sigma, divide the final latent by 0.18215 before VAE decoding, then map with image / 2 + 0.5 and clamp to [0, 1]. The number 0.18215 is the scaling factor of the tutorial's VAE and belongs to that autoencoder, so with a different VAE read the factor from its own configuration instead of copying the number.

5Practice

Exercise 1

Sample a two-point distribution with an exact denoiser and sweep the step count

CodingIntermediateAbout 45 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

The simplest distribution a diffusion model can learn is data that is exactly +1 or -1 with equal probability. For it the ideal denoiser has a closed form, so you can study sampling without training anything. With xt=αˉt x0+1−αˉt εx_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilonxt​=αˉt​​x0​+1−αˉt​​ε, the best guess of the clean value is x^0=tanh⁡ ⁣(αˉt xt/(1−αˉt))\hat{x}_0 = \tanh\!\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)\big)x^0​=tanh(αˉt​​xt​/(1−αˉt​)), and the exact noise prediction is ε^=(xt−αˉt x^0)/1−αˉt\hat\varepsilon = (x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat{x}_0)/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}ε^=(xt​−αˉt​​x^0​)/1−αˉt​​.

Starting code (standard library only, Python 3):

python
import math
import random

T = 1000
betas = [1e-4 + (0.02 - 1e-4) * i / (T - 1) for i in range(T)]   # beta_1 .. beta_T
abar = [1.0]                                                      # abar[t], with abar[0] = 1
for beta in betas:
    abar.append(abar[-1] * (1 - beta))


def forward_chain(x0, t, rng):
    """Add noise one step at a time: x_k = sqrt(1 - beta_k) x_{k-1} + sqrt(beta_k) eps."""
    x = x0
    for k in range(t):
        x = math.sqrt(1 - betas[k]) * x + math.sqrt(betas[k]) * rng.gauss(0, 1)
    return x


def eps_hat(x, t):
    """Exact noise prediction when the data is +1 or -1 with equal probability."""
    a = abar[t]
    x0_hat = math.tanh(math.sqrt(a) * x / (1 - a))   # E[x0 | x_t]
    return (x - math.sqrt(a) * x0_hat) / math.sqrt(1 - a)

Your tasks:

  1. Simulate the forward chain one small step at a time, from x0=0.8x_0 = 0.8x0​=0.8 for 250 steps, 20,000 times, and compare the sample mean and variance with the closed form 0.8αˉ2500.8\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{250}}0.8αˉ250​​ and 1−αˉ2501-\bar\alpha_{250}1−αˉ250​.
  2. Write sample(steps, eta, rng) using the DDIM update from the lesson on steps evenly spaced timesteps round(T * k / steps). Start from rng.gauss(0, 1). Set σ=η(1−αˉprev)/(1−αˉt) 1−αˉt/αˉprev\sigma = \eta\sqrt{(1-\bar\alpha_{prev})/(1-\bar\alpha_t)}\,\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t/\bar\alpha_{prev}}σ=η(1−αˉprev​)/(1−αˉt​)​1−αˉt​/αˉprev​​.
  3. For steps in 1000, 100, 20, 10, 5, 2 and eta in 0 and 1, draw 2,000 samples with a fresh random.Random(0) and print the mean distance from each sample to the nearest of -1 and +1, and the fraction of positive samples.
  4. Say in two sentences where quality starts to fall and whether eta changed the picture.

Requirements

  • Print the simulated mean and variance of the 250-step chain next to the closed-form values.
  • Implement the sampler with the DDIM update, including the final step that lands on the clean estimate.
  • Report both metrics for every combination of step count and eta, using the same seed for each setting.
  • Write the two-sentence conclusion, referring to your numbers.

Expected behaviour

The simulated chain should give a mean near 0.579 and a variance near 0.476 (0.576 and 0.479 with seed 0). The mean distance to the nearest mode should be essentially zero for 100 and 1000 steps, about 0.001 or less at 20 steps, about 0.03 at 10, about 0.25 to 0.29 at 5 and about 0.78 at 2. The fraction of positive samples should stay near 0.5 (between about 0.49 and 0.53 with 2,000 samples), showing that both modes are used.

Hint 1

Index the schedule so that abar[0] = 1 and abar[t] is the product of the first t values of 1 - beta. The last step of every sampler then lands on abar[0].

Hint 2

At each step compute eps_hat first, then x0_hat = (x - sqrt(1 - a) * e) / sqrt(a), then sigma, then the update. Wrap the square root of 1 - a_prev - sigma**2 in max(..., 0.0).

Hint 3

When t_prev is 0, abar_prev is 1 and sigma is 0, so the output of that step is exactly x0_hat.

Hint 4

Create a new random.Random(0) for each setting so every setting starts from the same noise.

Show solution

The code below follows the lesson's DDIM update. The only network in the loop is the exact denoiser, so every error you see comes from taking large steps.

python
import math
import random

T = 1000
betas = [1e-4 + (0.02 - 1e-4) * i / (T - 1) for i in range(T)]   # beta_1 .. beta_T
abar = [1.0]                                                      # abar[t], with abar[0] = 1
for beta in betas:
    abar.append(abar[-1] * (1 - beta))


def forward_chain(x0, t, rng):
    """Add noise one step at a time: x_k = sqrt(1 - beta_k) x_{k-1} + sqrt(beta_k) eps."""
    x = x0
    for k in range(t):
        x = math.sqrt(1 - betas[k]) * x + math.sqrt(betas[k]) * rng.gauss(0, 1)
    return x


def eps_hat(x, t):
    """Exact noise prediction when the data is +1 or -1 with equal probability."""
    a = abar[t]
    x0_hat = math.tanh(math.sqrt(a) * x / (1 - a))   # E[x0 | x_t]
    return (x - math.sqrt(a) * x0_hat) / math.sqrt(1 - a)


def sample(steps, eta, rng):
    """DDIM-style sampler over `steps` evenly spaced timesteps; eta=0 is deterministic."""
    ts = [round(T * k / steps) for k in range(steps, -1, -1)]   # T, ..., 0
    x = rng.gauss(0, 1)
    for t, t_prev in zip(ts[:-1], ts[1:]):
        a, a_prev = abar[t], abar[t_prev]
        e = eps_hat(x, t)
        x0_hat = (x - math.sqrt(1 - a) * e) / math.sqrt(a)
        sigma = eta * math.sqrt((1 - a_prev) / (1 - a)) * math.sqrt(1 - a / a_prev)
        x = (math.sqrt(a_prev) * x0_hat
             + math.sqrt(max(1 - a_prev - sigma ** 2, 0.0)) * e
             + sigma * rng.gauss(0, 1))
    return x


rng = random.Random(0)

# Part 1: the chain of 250 small steps matches the closed form.
runs = [forward_chain(0.8, 250, rng) for _ in range(20000)]
mean = sum(runs) / len(runs)
var = sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in runs) / len(runs)
print(f"chain      mean={mean:.3f} var={var:.3f}")
print(f"closed form mean={math.sqrt(abar[250]) * 0.8:.3f} var={1 - abar[250]:.3f}")

# Part 2: sweep the number of sampling steps.
print("steps  eta  distance_to_mode  fraction_positive")
for steps in (1000, 100, 20, 10, 5, 2):
    for eta in (0.0, 1.0):
        rng = random.Random(0)
        xs = [sample(steps, eta, rng) for _ in range(2000)]
        dist = sum(min(abs(v - 1), abs(v + 1)) for v in xs) / len(xs)
        pos = sum(v > 0 for v in xs) / len(xs)
        print(f"{steps:5d}  {eta:.0f}    {dist:.4f}            {pos:.3f}")

Output with Python 3.13 (the exact digits can differ slightly on other versions or seeds):

text
chain      mean=0.576 var=0.479
closed form mean=0.579 var=0.476
steps  eta  distance_to_mode  fraction_positive
 1000  0    0.0000            0.500
 1000  1    0.0000            0.525
  100  0    0.0000            0.486
  100  1    0.0000            0.506
   20  0    0.0007            0.501
   20  1    0.0001            0.508
   10  0    0.0323            0.510
   10  1    0.0351            0.505
    5  0    0.2454            0.486
    5  1    0.2853            0.508
    2  0    0.7816            0.505
    2  1    0.7741            0.505

Reading the numbers: the chain simulation matches the closed form to about 0.003, which is the Monte Carlo error for 20,000 runs. Quality is essentially perfect down to 20 steps, starts to fall at 10 steps (distance about 0.03), and collapses at 5 and 2 steps, even though the denoiser is exact. With a perfect network the only remaining error is the discretisation error of taking big steps, which is what a step-count sweep measures. In this toy eta barely matters, so the large gap between eta = 0 and eta = 1 in the DDIM paper's CIFAR-10 table cannot come from step size alone; this toy leaves out the errors of a learned network and the complexity of real images.

Check your answer

  • Does your chain simulation give a mean near 0.579 and a variance near 0.476?
  • Is the mean distance to the nearest mode below 0.001 at 100 and 1000 steps and above 0.7 at 2 steps?
  • Does each setting put roughly half of the samples on each mode?
  • Can you explain why quality drops at few steps even though the denoiser is exact?

Exercise 2

Budget the denoiser evaluations of three diffusion systems

AnalysisIntermediateAbout 30 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

A team wants to compare the inference cost of three documented systems in denoiser evaluations, meaning one forward pass of the network, counting the extra pass that guidance adds. Use only the figures in this lesson.

  • A. The Stable Diffusion pipeline at its documented defaults: 50 steps, guidance_scale 7.5.
  • B. The SDXL-Turbo example from its model card: 1 step, guidance_scale 0.0.
  • C. One GenCast ensemble member: 30 forecast steps, each using 20 solver steps of a second-order solver that needs two evaluations per solver step, except the last one, which needs one.

Tasks:

  1. Compute the evaluations per image for A and B and per ensemble member for C, then for a 50-member ensemble.
  2. For A, compute how many values the U-Net processes per evaluation for a 512×512 RGB image in pixel space and for a 64×64×4 latent, and the ratio.
  3. A product owner caps system A at 20 evaluations per image. Give two different ways to meet the cap and the quality risk of each, using evidence from the lesson.
  4. In three or four sentences, explain why evaluations are an imperfect proxy for latency.

Requirements

  • Show the arithmetic for A, B and C in a small table.
  • State your assumption about whether guidance counts as one evaluation or two per step.
  • Give two distinct options for the 20-evaluation cap and one concrete risk for each.

Expected behaviour

A is 50 × 2 = 100 evaluations, B is 1, and C is 30 × 39 = 1,170 per member and 58,500 for 50 members. The pixel array has 512 × 512 × 3 = 786,432 values and the latent 64 × 64 × 4 = 16,384, a ratio of 48. Two valid ways to meet the cap are 10 steps with guidance (20 evaluations) and 20 steps with guidance off (20 evaluations).

Hint 1

Guidance with a scale above 1 needs both a conditional and an unconditional prediction at every step.

Hint 2

For C, the second-order solver uses 2 × 20 − 1 evaluations per forecast step, and 15 days at 12 hours per step is 30 steps.

Hint 3

For the cap, look at the DDIM bar chart for what a low step count costs, and at what guidance_scale 0.0 means for prompt control.

Show solution
SystemStepsEvaluations per stepEvaluations
A: Stable Diffusion defaults502 (guidance on)100
B: SDXL-Turbo example11 (guidance off)1
C: one GenCast member30 forecast steps39 per forecast step1,170
C: 50-member ensemble50 × 303958,500

Assumption: guidance counts as two evaluations per step even though Diffusers batches them into one call, because the network still processes twice as many inputs. The latent has 16,384 values against 786,432 pixel values, so the U-Net handles 48 times fewer values per evaluation (assuming four latent channels).

Meeting a cap of 20 evaluations for A: (1) use 10 steps with guidance. The risk is the quality loss that fewer steps bring, shown in the lesson by the DDIM paper's CIFAR-10 FID of 13.36 at 10 steps against 4.04 at 1000 for the deterministic sampler (a different model and data set, so it shows the direction, not the size). (2) Use 20 steps and switch guidance off. The risk is weaker prompt adherence, since guidance is what pushes the sample towards the prompt. A third option is to swap in a distilled few-step model, at the cost of the limitations on its model card.

Evaluations are an imperfect proxy because networks differ in size: SDXL-Turbo is built on SDXL, and the ADD paper lists its SDXL-based ADD-XL model at 3.1 billion parameters while the Stable Diffusion U-Net in A has 860 million, so one evaluation is not the same amount of work in the two systems and B is not simply 100 times faster. Guidance passes are batched, so they use memory and arithmetic in parallel rather than running twice in sequence. Ensemble members, as the GenCast post says, can run in parallel on more hardware, so total evaluations measure cost, not elapsed time. Finally, decoding with the VAE and encoding the prompt add work outside the loop.

Check your answer

  • Did you count 100, 1 and 1,170 evaluations for A, B and C, and 58,500 for the ensemble?
  • Did you state whether guidance counts as one or two evaluations per step?
  • Do your two ways to meet the cap each name a different quality risk?
  • Did you explain why equal evaluation counts would not mean equal latency?
